paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: the LORD wins the battle, and He lets people show up for it. Israel had nine hundred chariots of iron pressing down on them for twenty years, and the LORD still told Barak, "Go and march to Mount Tabor." Then Deborah says, "Has not the LORD gone before you?" (Judges 4:6, 14). The LORD went first, and Barak's job was to come down the mountain.

The song makes the same point from the other side, because Zebulun and Naphtali "risked their lives" (Judges 5:18). But of Reuben it says, "great indecision," and the angel of the LORD says of Meroz that they "did not come to help the LORD" (Judges 5:15, 23). I think that stings a little, because we all know what it's like to read the message and not move. When the LORD says go, the song treats showing up as something worth singing about.

And look at who the LORD used: a prophetess under a palm tree, a man who wanted her to come along, and Jael, a woman in a tent, just as Deborah said the LORD would sell Sisera "into the hand of a woman" (Judges 4:9). You don't have to be the commander with the iron chariots, baker. The song ends asking that "those who love You shine like the sun at its brightest" (Judges 5:31). So when He says go, go, because He's already ahead of you.
